toc.title: What it's already been used for
A predictor, and a chance to help early

blocks.p: If you're reading this, you're a fellow polyvagal nerd. You already understand the basic idea of the autonomic nervous system. It directly regulates our abilities to connect with each other, to mobilize, to immobilize, and more. Our state provides the foundation for our thoughts, our emotions, our impulses, and our sensations.

But you might not know about vagal efficiency. It's been around for a few years, I believe, but it's not something we discuss within the typical Polyvagal Theory topics. I think it's an important concept. So get ready for probably the deepest dive into polyvagal nerdery you've taken outside of Dr. Porges's own work. I want to teach you what vagal efficiency is, and how to get more of it.
The first thing to understand is the vagal brake. A really quick recap: the vagal brake is the influence of the safety state on your heart, through the myelinated ventral vagal pathways.
In her book Polyvagal Theory in Therapy, Deb Dana says:

q: The vagal brake is designed to release and re-engage as a way of responding to challenges while still maintaining ventral vagal regulation. Once the autonomic challenge is met the vagal brake recovers, reengages and returns the system to balance.

blocks.p: She goes on to say, "This is a commonly experienced pattern throughout the course of a day as we energize to meet the demands of the multiple and often conflicting needs dictated by work and family schedules." And finally: "When the ventral vagal system cannot meet the needs for safety, the vagal brake releases, allowing the sympathetic nervous system to come into full activation."

Long quote, but basically what it means is this. When the brake is active, the heart beats at a calmer pace. The vagal brake is important for being calm, for being relaxed, and for soothing other people through co-regulation. When it's released, it allows for mobilization, more of a sympathetic, flight or fight influence. The way we measure it is through respiratory sinus arrhythmia, or RSA.
The vagal brake is not a thing. I don't want you to imagine a flap or anything like that. It's the influence of the safety state.

Vagal efficiency is a metric for the efficiency of the vagal brake. It measures how well the vagal brake is working: how well your ventral vagal system, which regulates your heart rate, is keeping your heart at a calmer pace. More specifically, it tells us how efficiently your body can adjust your heart rate in response to different situations.

Here's a metaphor. Imagine your heart is a car engine. When you need to slow down or relax, the ventral vagus presses on a metaphorical brake pedal, which slows your heart rate. That helps you feel calm and relaxed. When you need to speed up or be more alert, the ventral vagus releases the brake pedal, letting your heart rate increase. That helps you feel more energized and ready to take action.

Vagal efficiency is like the responsiveness of that brake pedal. If the pedal is very sensitive and quickly adjusts the speed of the car, we'd say the car is highly efficient in braking. If it's slow to respond or doesn't work properly, the car has low efficiency.

The same is true in our bodies. If your ventral vagal system is efficient, it can quickly and accurately adjust your heart rate to match the needs of your body. In other words, the safety state is strong enough to adjust heart rate to meet the needs of the environment. If your ventral vagal safety system is not efficient, it may have trouble regulating your heart rate effectively. That makes it difficult both to calm down when needed and to become more alert when needed.
So, as best I understand it, vagal efficiency is like the efficiency of the brake pedal in a car: how well your ventral vagal system can adjust your heart rate in different situations.
The next question might be: how is this measured? Vagal efficiency is evaluated through the slope of the regression line between heart rate and respiratory sinus arrhythmia.

If you're like me, you don't know what that means. That's polyvagal research territory, and I can't take it deeper than that right now, unfortunately. Dr. Porges and the polyvagal researchers have a way of measuring it that I honestly don't fully understand, but it has to do with respiratory sinus arrhythmia. What I do know is that, the way it's calculated, it tells us how effectively the vagal brake can handle our heart rate based on what our body needs at any given moment.

blocks.h: What it's already been used for

blocks.p: The practical applications are pretty diverse. All of these come from primary Polyvagal Theory research papers:

ul: It's been used to evaluate sleep states in newborns.
It's been used to track the development of preterm infants.
It might serve as an indicator of dysautonomia, a condition characterized by impaired autonomic nervous system functioning.
Lower vagal efficiency has been studied in individuals with a history of adversity.
It's been studied in people with certain medical conditions, such as the hypermobility subtype of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

blocks.p: Vagal efficiency could potentially be a way of seeing what's happening ventral vagally underneath each of these groups.

There are some pretty interesting possibilities for the future, if this can be used as a practical measurement of vagal brake strength. I don't think we're there yet. But maybe at some point it could be measured through our smartwatches. Our watches can already measure heart rate, heart rate variability, and blood oxygenation, so I have no doubt that at some point this will be pretty easy to measure. I don't know what that looks like.

If it were, it could be a way of measuring success. We can already feel these changes subjectively. We can feel when we have more safety state activation, when we feel more connected to the present moment or to the people in our lives. Vagal efficiency would be an objective measure that could show someone, "Hey, you are making progress."

As a therapist, and in my trauma recovery courses, I would love to have that objective number to give to somebody, or for them to see on a wearable. The people who come to me already have a weaker vagal brake, and therefore, I assume, lower vagal efficiency. Through the work, they can feel and notice change. But an objective measure would make it a lot more real.

It's like losing weight. If your goal is to lose weight, you can measure it on a scale to validate your progress. You don't need to. You might look in the mirror and notice you look different, or notice you feel different day to day. There are ways to validate it without the measurement. But the measurement takes it further, if that's something you want.

blocks.h: A predictor, and a chance to help early

blocks.p: I asked Dr. Porges about this when I interviewed him in episode 201. Vagal efficiency could be used as a predictor of future health, and even of emotional regulation or behavioral concerns.

What if we could measure vagal efficiency at birth, or throughout life during regular doctor visits, and see that someone's vagal efficiency is way low? If we see that in a baby, that's an opportunity to tell parents how important healthy attachment is, and meeting the needs of their child. It's an opportunity to educate and encourage them and give them resources. As parents bond with their kids in a healthier way, my assumption is that the child's vagal brake strength would increase, because their safety state increases.

Hopefully every parent already has that message, but realistically, not everybody does. Maybe there's a parent who's open to "Maybe I need to do something about myself to help the future of my child." If a doctor could say early on, "Look, this vagal efficiency is really concerning. It could lead to potential behavior problems, health problems, or emotional regulation problems," maybe that parent could get the resources to form a healthy attachment with their baby. Hopefully then we'd see better health outcomes, not just for that child, but on a larger scale too. I don't know how far along they are in being able to measure vagal efficiency efficiently for the general population.

Something I've found in my reading is that there seems to be a correlation between positive engagement and more vagal efficiency, and a correlation with quicker respiratory sinus arrhythmia recovery. RSA is a measurement of ventral vagal, safety state activation. So basically, this suggests that things that feel good correlate with more RSA, with more safety state activation.
Attachment, a safe environment, and co-regulation all help to increase vagal brake strength, and likely would increase vagal efficiency as well.
You probably can't track your vagal efficiency or your vagal brake strength directly. But you can:

ol: Notice when you're in your safety state.
Practice moments of mindfulness and connection every day, even with yourself or with the external environment.
Do things that bring you an overall experience of positivity and connection.

blocks.p: As you practice these, they will eventually increase your vagal brake strength, and presumably your vagal efficiency as well.

So, for now, I'd really encourage you to have at least micro moments of mindfulness and micro moments of connection. Practice them as often as you can. Work on building the strength of your safety state, which leads to greater strength in your vagal brake, and presumably more vagal efficiency too.
